source: Schoenfeld (1979) Explicit heuristic training as a variable in problem-solving performance (JRME 10(3))
finding: Primary paper now opened. Seven upper-division science and maths majors at Berkeley. Four randomly chosen got training in five heuristics, three got problem-solving practice without heuristics. The heuristic group improved, the control group did not.
numbers: N=7 (4 vs 3). All 4 heuristic students improved from pretest to posttest, only 1 of 3 controls did. Mean net gain: controls 0, heuristic group more than 2 problems. All 4 heuristic students outscored all 3 controls; chance 1/35, p<.05. Posttest problems cut off at 20 minutes.
quote: all four of the students who received heuristics training outscored all three who did not
limits: Tiny N, exact permutation p only, no no-training group, five heuristics trained together so no per-heuristic effect, problems chosen to fit the taught heuristics.
agent_relevance: Closes the primary-source part of gap 5. The human heuristic effect is real but rests on 7 people. Use as motivation, not as an effect size for our agent.

source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) Explizites oder implizites Heurismentraining - was ist besser? (Mathematica Didactica 37)
finding: Replication of Schoenfeld 1979 with improved design. 28 teacher-education students in three groups: explicit heuristic training plus problem solving, problem-solving training only, and no training. Five heuristics, pretest and posttest. The combined explicit training won.
numbers: N=28 (9 explicit, 10 practice-only, 9 no training). Raw points 43 pre, 40 post. Posttest ANOVA F=3.853, p=.035; explicit vs practice-only p=.043 (Bonferroni). Gain scores F=6.307, p=.006; explicit vs no training p=.005. Corrected d: explicit vs practice 0.786, explicit vs none 1.438, practice vs none 0.640. Explicit group gained almost 4 raw points; no-training group lost almost 4 (16 to 12). Only the explicit group gained significantly within group.
limits: Small groups, German student teachers, short training, posttest slightly harder than pretest (no-training group fell), effect sizes from an online calculator, no per-heuristic breakdown.
agent_relevance: First quantified human replication of heuristic training: medium to large d (0.79 to 1.44) with small N. Naming a heuristic and when to use it beat practice alone. Supports an explicit heuristic menu with use-conditions in the schema, with caution.

source: Hembree (1992) Experiments and relational studies in problem solving: a meta-analysis (JRME 23(2):242-273), with Goldin critique and Hembree reply (23(3):284-289)
finding: Could not open the text. Publisher and aggregator pages were blocked and the search quota ran out. Only bibliographic facts were seen in a search snippet: the paper was criticised by Goldin and Hembree replied, defending meta-analysis against concerns about disparate measures and missing theory.
numbers: No effect sizes read this session.
limits: Unread. Do not cite any Hembree effect size.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for the meta-analytic effect size of heuristic instruction. Needs a library copy or a citing review that quotes the number.

source: Mevarech and Kramarski (1997) IMPROVE metacognitive questioning, and follow-up effect sizes
finding: Not opened. No open full text was reachable and searches were blocked after the quota ran out.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for IMPROVE effect sizes.

source: Sun, Tang, Li, Maddison and Meel (2025) Enumerate-Conjecture-Prove: formally solving answer-construction problems in math competitions
finding: First LLM test of Polya's specialise-then-conjecture loop on competition maths. The LLM enumerates small cases, conjectures a pattern, then a Lean prover checks it. Large gain over plain chain of thought on answer-construction problems.
numbers: ConstructiveBench: 3,431 formalised problems (64.6% of 5,316). Answer accuracy CoT vs ECP: gpt-4.1-mini 14.54 to 45.06; gpt-4.1-nano 17.02 to 32.59; deepseek-v3 19.06 to 43.81. Post-cutoff subset (92 problems): mini 5.43 to 31.52. PutnamBench 337 answer-construction problems: mini 15.13 to 23.15, deepseek-v3 18.99 to 31.75. Proving with DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B: 858 of 3,431 (25.01%) vs 9.86% symbolic-only.
quote: enumeration and pattern-driven conjecturing with formal theorem proving
limits: Non-reasoning base models; CoT baseline limited to 2,048 tokens and Pass@32 proving; no token-matched baseline; no ablation of enumeration alone vs conjecture alone; authors note enumeration explodes on hard IMO problems; tasks are find-the-object, not proofs.
agent_relevance: Closes most of gap 4: specialise (enumerate small cases) then conjecture helps a lot on find-the-answer problems, including post-cutoff ones. Untested: reasoning models, equal tokens, proof problems.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick and Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The decreasing value of chain of thought in prompting
finding: On GPQA Diamond (198 questions, 25 trials each) a step-by-step prompt gives only marginal accuracy gains on reasoning models but costs more time. Many non-reasoning models already do CoT by default, so the prompt adds little there too.
numbers: Reasoning models, CoT vs direct: o3-mini +2.9 points (p=.024), o4-mini +3.1 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -3.3 (p=.005); time +20 to 80%. Non-reasoning, CoT vs direct: Flash 2.0 +13.5, Sonnet 3.5 +11.7, GPT-4o-mini +4.4 (ns). Against the default no-prompt condition gains mostly vanish (Flash 2.0 +6.2, GPT-4o +6.9, Sonnet 3.5 -1.9 ns). CoT lowered the strict 25-of-25 correct rate for 3 of 5 non-reasoning models.
quote: For dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: One benchmark (science multiple choice, not proofs), one simple prompt. Three richer variants (think carefully, decompose then weigh paths, weigh three paths) were tested on GPT-4o and gave negligible differences.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: generic reasoning prompts add little for reasoning models. A heuristic scaffold must beat that bar at equal tokens. A 'decompose, consider paths, pick' variant gave no meaningful gain on GPT-4o.

source: Elenjical, Kavuri and Varma (2026) Think2: grounded metacognitive reasoning in LLMs (Ann Brown planning, monitoring, evaluation prompt)
finding: Closest direct test of a forced monitoring step (gap 1). Forcing Plan, Monitor, Evaluate on every query hurts a non-reasoning 8B model on GSM8K and is neutral on a reasoning 8B model. Self-correction on seeded errors improved, but on only 24 tracked errors.
numbers: Llama-3-8B GSM8K: standard 80.71, CoT 77.98, Metacognitive Prompting 74.26, Ann Brown 69.55. Qwen-3-8B (thinking) GSM8K: 91.72, 90.89, 88.38, 91.65; AIME 4.82, 4.93, 5.57, 5.89; MBPP 74.94, 85.25, 73.07, 79.39 (CoT best). Self-correction funnel: Ann Brown 12 of 24 errors improved (50.0%) vs 7 of 43 for all baselines (16.3%), CoT 3 of 12 (25.0%). Blinded human preference 84.1% (580 pairs). A routing MetaController (apply only when needed) recovered some loss, e.g. CRUXEval-O 55.88 to 57.88.
limits: 8B models only; generation capped at 2,048 tokens; AIME near 5% so differences are noise-level; funnel counts are tiny; no token-matched control; human preference is not accuracy; preprint, code not yet released.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 half-closed: forced monitoring is not free. On a non-reasoning model it cost 11 points on GSM8K; on a reasoning model it is roughly neutral on accuracy. Supports a conditional monitor (fires at junctures or on stall), not one on every step.

source: Silver, Sun, Zhang, Hooker and Kim (2025) Language models can perform single-utterance self-correction of perturbed reasoning
finding: Wrong steps were planted in the model's own chain of thought (GSM8K, MATH-500). The large reasoning model R1 recovered almost fully. Non-reasoning models recovered partly, with 'wait' or 'however' pivots appearing without special training.
numbers: Excluding R1, average absolute success-rate drop with an on-policy perturbation 61.6 points; models under 30B drop 78.1, over 30B drop 41.7. R1 671B recovery about 90 across datasets and scenarios. Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3.3-70B roughly match QwQ-32B on MATH-500.
limits: Synthetic perturbations, not natural errors; open-weight models; says nothing about whether a prompt can elicit more.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a large reasoning model already carries its own monitor, so an external monitor adds less there. Small models do not recover and need scaffolding. Also qualifies K13 (intrinsic self-correction fails), which was measured on 2023 instruct models.

source: Wang et al. (2025) On the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: The opposite of repeated-strategy failure. o1-like models switch thoughts too often on hard problems and finish none. Wrong answers use far more tokens and switches. Penalising switch tokens at decode time raised accuracy a little.
numbers: Incorrect responses used 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones (QwQ-32B-Preview, R1). Underthinking score AIME24: QwQ 65.0, R1-671B 37.0. With the switch penalty, Pass@1: QwQ AIME24 38.3 to 44.1, GPQA Diamond 57.6 to 59.1, MATH500-Hard 83.1 to 83.7; R1-Distill-32B AIME24 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8. A prompt telling R1 to stay on one thought gave 72.4, below the 73.8 baseline.
limits: Switch count is correlational; the penalty needs logit access; gains are small except QwQ on AIME24; thoughts are split on marker words such as 'alternatively'.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: forced strategy switching is not free and may hurt. For reasoning models the failure is shallow exploration, not stubbornness. The schema needs a depth-before-switch rule (switch only after a bounded attempt fails a stated check), not a blanket 'try another approach'.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on the 2025 USA Math Olympiad (re-read for strategy behaviour)
finding: Re-opened the strategy paragraph. Models often tried the same wrong strategy across all attempts. One model (Flash Thinking) tried several strategies within a run but explored each only shallowly. Both patterns failed.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Pro 24.4% average (solved, 6/7 or more, in 6 of its 24 attempts); every other model under 5%. Scores averaged over 4 runs, 6 problems, 7 points each.
limits: Human-graded; no intervention was tried, so the paper cannot say whether forcing a switch helps; error taxonomy is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: both failure modes are observed (repeat one strategy, or switch with no depth). No study tests forced switching on proofs, so the question stays open. d09 suggests blanket switching alone will not fix it.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners, appendix H (transfer to other domains)
finding: Appendix H holds the only transfer test. Behaviours amplified by math-style pretraining curation appear much more often on GPQA questions, but accuracy does not change.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B with curated pretraining vs behaviour-minimised control, 200 GPQA questions: subgoal setting 6.5 vs 0.7 instances per question; all four behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) more frequent; accuracy about 12% in both. Main text: empty-CoT priming left Llama at 30 to 35% on Countdown; Qwen reached about 60% vs Llama 30% after RL.
quote: the model is limited in its forward inference capabilities rather than its problem-solving strategy
limits: Transfer is of behaviour counts, not solve rate; 3B models; Countdown-only RL; no GSM8K or proof test; training, not prompting. Main text says models primed with incorrect solutions that show the right behaviours perform comparably (not identically) to those primed with correct ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: behaviours transfer as habits but did not raise accuracy on a hard knowledge benchmark, and no pure-scaffolding test exists. A scaffold may induce the habits, but the ceiling is set by the model.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention (is something you might need too)
finding: Gap 9: an explicit step that regenerates the context with only the relevant parts, before solving. On GSM-IC distractor problems it beat both the baseline and an 'ignore irrelevant text' instruction.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B-chat, GSM-IC 100 problems, 3 seeds, zero-shot: in-topic distractors 51.7% to 61.3% with the regenerate step; random distractors about +12 points. Instructed prompting ('ignore irrelevant sentences') gave no consistent improvement. Opinion-laden factual QA 62.8% to 80.3%.
limits: Old chat model, 100 problems, two-call pipeline (more tokens), no reasoning models, no GSM-NoOp test.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed for 2023 models: restate-and-strip works as an explicit step, a bare instruction did not. Needs a re-test on reasoning models (see d13).

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats confuse reasoning LLM: query-agnostic adversarial triggers for reasoning models (CatAttack)
finding: Appending an irrelevant sentence ('cats sleep most of their lives') to maths problems raises the error rate of reasoning models. A plain 'ignore distracting statements' instruction helped a small non-reasoning model a lot.
numbers: More than 300% increase in wrong answers for DeepSeek R1 and R1-distill-Qwen-32B; up to 500% for reasoning models and 700% for instruction-tuned models across QwQ, Qwen3, Phi-4, Llama-3.1, Mistral. Defense on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: instruction to ignore distracting statements cut combined attack success rate from 37.5% to 9.9%; SFT on two triggers failed to generalise to a third.
limits: Triggers were selected on a proxy model (DeepSeek V3); base error rates are low so relative increases look large; defense tested on one 8B model only; no restate step tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: brittleness persists in 2025 reasoning models. The cheapest defense (instruction to ignore) worked here but not in d12 (older model), so the effect depends on the model: test it, do not assume it.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic, few-shot recovery controls on GSM-NoOp (re-read)
finding: Re-opened the few-shot controls. Giving 8 solved variants of the same question, or 8 NoOp examples, did not fix the drop. No restate-and-strip step was tested.
numbers: GSM-NoOp drops: Phi-3-mini over 65%, o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o-mini -40.0.
limits: Few-shot examples are not the same as a restate step. Models turn statements such as 'discount' into multiplication without checking context.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: in-context examples do not fix this brittleness. A procedural check (d12) is a different intervention, still untested on GSM-NoOp itself.

source: Zhao, Awasthi and Gollapudi (2025) Sample, scrutinize and scale: effective inference-time search by scaling verification
finding: Gap 8: voting vs verification at scale. Self-consistency saturates, while self-verification of many samples keeps improving, because a larger pool also makes verification easier (implicit scaling).
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro on AIME: Consistency@50 equals Consistency@10,000; Verification@k shows power-law scaling with 50 verification attempts fixed. Example: of 200 samples for one AIME problem only one was right (601); consistency chose '1' (over half the samples); verification scored the right one 98% and the wrong one 36%. Out-of-box verification of frontier models was 'remarkably weak' on their benchmark.
limits: Compute is not matched to a single-sample budget; verification here is a model rereading the answer, not backward reasoning; Gemini 1.5-era models; AIME has only 15 problems per exam.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 half-closed: more verification beats more voting at large budgets, but nobody has compared FOBAR-style backward checks with an extra sample at matched tokens on a strong model (d16).

source: Jiang et al. (2024) FOBAR: re-read of the compute design
finding: Re-opened the setup. The number of forward chains is identical for Self-Consistency, Self-Verification and FOBAR, and FOBAR adds backward chains, so FOBAR uses more tokens than self-consistency by design.
numbers: GPT-4 gain over self-consistency stays 0.3 points as in K12.
limits: No equal-token control in the paper, so a 0.3 gain could be bought equally by a few extra forward samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. A matched-token test (backward check vs extra independent sample) is a cheap experiment for us to run.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling (budget forcing with 'Wait')
finding: Appending 'Wait' to the model's own trace forces an extra re-check. It is the closest large-model test of forcing a verification step, though it is continuation, not a strategy change.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24 50% to 57% when the end of thinking is ignored up to 6 times. Sequential scaling beats majority voting of the base Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct over 2 to 64 votes (confounded: fine-tuned vs base). Forcing too often causes repetitive loops.
limits: Not token-matched. The sequential-vs-parallel comparison compares different models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 3, 8: a forced re-check helps for a few repeats, then loops. Cap the number of forced re-checks.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover (results and design, re-read for per-item choice)
finding: Gap 2: Self-Discover picks reasoning modules once per task from 39 seed modules, not per item, and compares with an oracle 'best of each module'. So per-item heuristic choice remains untested.
numbers: MATH (200 samples): PaLM 2-L 45%, CoT 42%, plan-and-solve 49%, Self-Discover 50.5%; GPT-4 70.5%, CoT 71%, PS 70%, Self-Discover 73%. BBH GPT-4 75% (CoT) to 81%; T4D GPT-4 52% to 85%. Select/adapt/implement ablation on only 4 tasks.
limits: Per-task selection; no per-heuristic ablation; largest gain on T4D (social reasoning) and BBH; MATH gain 2 to 5 points.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: no study ablates specialise, generalise, backward, analogy and decompose on one benchmark with per-item choice.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Absolute Zero: reinforced self-play reasoning with zero data (self-proposed tasks as an analogue of problem posing)
finding: Gap 10, indirect. A model that proposes its own problems, rewarded for learnability, trains a stronger solver than one with an untrained proposer. This is training-time problem posing, not Brown and Walter's 'what if not' on open tasks.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B base ablation: untrained proposer lowers the overall average from 46.8 to 45.4 (math 38.4 to 36.0); a fixed proposal prompt without reference conditioning drops math by 5 points and code by 1. Cross-domain: training on code-only self-proposed tasks lifts math average by 10.9 (Base-7B) and 15.2 (Coder-7B) vs 0.65 for expert code models.
limits: RL training on code reasoning tasks; no attribute-change operator; no inference-time scaffold test; single run per row.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Weak hint that proposing variants helps learning; no evidence a posing step helps a frozen agent at inference.
